chapters.title: Organisational Behaviour: Significance and Theories
chapters.scope: What organisational behaviour studies, and how management thought moved from efficiency to people to systems and situations.

blocks.title: What organisational behaviour studies
blocks.html:
Organisational behaviour (OB) studies how people think, feel and act at work: as individuals, in groups, and as part of the whole organisation. Its use is practical: to understand behaviour, predict it, and improve how people and organisations perform.

The management thought behind it moved in three steps: from efficiency, to human behaviour, to systems and situational thinking.

SchoolMain focusKey thinkers and theories
ClassicalEfficiency and structureTaylor, Fayol, Weber
BehaviouralPeople and motivationMayo, Maslow, McGregor
ModernSystems and adapting to the situationSystems theory, contingency theory

blocks.title: Classical school of management
blocks.html:
The classical school grew up with the Industrial Revolution. It stressed efficiency, organisational structure, division of work and a clear chain of command.

ApproachThinkerCore idea
Scientific managementF. W. TaylorUse scientific methods to find the most efficient way to do a job.
Administrative managementHenri FayolThe management process and general principles of management.
Bureaucratic managementMax WeberA formal organisation run by rules: clear hierarchy, detailed rules and regulations, clear division of labour, a formalised system of operation, impersonality and appointment by professional competence.

Taylor's four principles: science, not rule of thumb; scientific selection and training of workers; cooperation between workers and management; and division of work and responsibility, with managers planning and training and workers performing.

Fayol named five functions of management (planning, organising, commanding, coordinating and controlling) and fourteen principles, among them division of work, authority, discipline, unity of command and unity of direction. Weber's aim was efficiency and an end to favouritism.

blocks.title: Behavioural school of management
blocks.html:
The behavioural school was a reaction to the limits of the classical approach. It put human behaviour and social needs at the centre.

  • Hawthorne studies (Elton Mayo, at Western Electric's Hawthorne plant): productivity rose when employees felt valued; social needs, morale and relationships shape behaviour at work. The Hawthorne effect: attention and social relations change behaviour and productivity.
  • Maslow's hierarchy of needs: physiological, safety, social, esteem and self-actualisation. Managers should understand and address employees' different needs.
  • McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y: two opposite sets of assumptions about people at work.
Theory XTheory Y
View of workEmployees dislike workEmployees can be motivated
DirectionPeople need coercion and controlPeople can direct themselves and seek responsibility
StyleManagement-centred controlParticipative management
TrustLowTrust and collaboration
CreativityAssumed to be limitedEncouraged

The core contrast: control against participation.

blocks.title: Modern school: systems and contingency
blocks.html:
The modern school recognises how complex organisations are, and how much they depend on their environment.

Systems theory sees the organisation as an open system. Inputs (labour, materials, capital) pass through a transformation process (activities and operations) to become outputs (products and services), and feedback returns to the start, all within an external environment. The parts are interrelated and work toward a common goal; the key ideas are interdependence, interaction, environment and feedback.

Contingency theory holds that there is no single best way to manage: practice must be tailored to the situation. Effectiveness depends on the external environment, technology, organisational structure and the characteristics of the workforce. The manager analyses the situation, identifies the variables, adapts the practice and acts.

It depends on the situation.

text: Kauṭilya's accounts office (akṣapaṭala) keeps registers for every department, fixes when and how accounts are to be presented, and sets penalties for officials who fail to present them. Written records, set procedures and regular checks are what Weber later described as bureaucracy.
pairings.quote: Arthaśāstra 2.7

text: Theory Y assumes that people can direct themselves and will seek responsibility. The Gītā asks each person to raise themselves by their own effort and not let themselves sink, which treats self-direction as a human capacity. The verse is about inner discipline, not about a manager's assumptions.
pairings.quote: “Lift yourself by yourself; do not let yourself sink.” उद्धरेदात्मनात्मानं नात्मानमवसादयेत् । uddhared ātmanātmānaṃ nātmānam avasādayet. Bhagavad Gītā 6.5

chapters.title: Personality, Perception and Attitude
chapters.scope: Who a person is, how they read the world, and the stance they take toward it: three building blocks of individual behaviour at work.

blocks.title: Personality
blocks.html:
Personality is the unique and relatively consistent pattern of a person's thoughts, emotions and behaviour. It is shaped by genetics, environment, experience and learning, and it matters at work for recruitment, communication, team dynamics, leadership, motivation, job satisfaction and performance.

The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI), developed by Katharine Briggs and Isabel Myers from Carl Jung's psychological types, sorts people into 16 types along four dimensions. It is used to understand team compatibility, leadership styles and communication preferences.

DimensionOne preferenceThe other
E – IExtraversion: interaction, outward energyIntroversion: reflection, solitude
S – NSensing: facts and present realitiesIntuition: patterns and possibilities
T – FThinking: logic and objectivityFeeling: empathy and human impact
J – PJudging: structure and decisivenessPerceiving: flexibility and spontaneity
TheoryProponentsCore idea
PsychoanalyticSigmund FreudUnconscious conflicts among id, ego and superego; early childhood shapes personality.
BehaviouristB. F. Skinner, J. B. WatsonPersonality develops through learning, conditioning and reinforcement.
HumanisticCarl Rogers, Abraham MaslowPeople strive for self-growth and to fulfil their potential.
TraitGordon Allport; the Big FivePersonality is a set of relatively stable traits.
CognitiveAlbert BanduraMental processes, observation, imitation and self-efficacy shape personality.
BiologicalHans Eysenck; Darwinian viewPersonality is linked to genetics, brain chemistry and evolution.

The Big Five (OCEAN): openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism.

blocks.title: Perception
blocks.html:
Perception is the process of selecting, organising and interpreting sensory information to give meaning to the environment. It is subjective: the same situation can draw different responses because people's experiences and expectations differ.

StageWhat happens
1 SelectionWe notice only some of the many stimuli, influenced by intensity, relevance, novelty, interests and expectations.
2 OrganisationWe arrange what we noticed into patterns, by similarity, proximity and closure.
3 InterpretationWe give it meaning using experience, beliefs and motives. Assumptions and stereotypes creep in here.

Three sets of factors shape perception: the perceiver (motives, experiences, attitudes, expectations), the target (appearance, behaviour, communication style) and the situation (context, time, work setting).

Perceptual errorWhat happens
StereotypingJudging a person by the group they belong to.
Halo effectOne favourable trait shapes the whole judgement.
Horn effectOne unfavourable trait shapes the whole judgement.
Selective perceptionNoticing only what supports opinions already held.
ProjectionAttributing one's own thoughts, feelings or motives to others.
Contrast effectJudging a person against others rather than against an objective standard.

blocks.title: Attitude
blocks.html:
An attitude is a learned tendency to respond consistently, in a favourable or unfavourable way. It combines beliefs, feelings and an intention to behave, and it influences job satisfaction, motivation and organisational commitment.

ComponentWhat it isExample
AffectiveFeelings and emotions: liking, disliking, indifference“I enjoy this project.”
BehaviouralAn intention or readiness to actWorking overtime to reach a goal
CognitiveBeliefs and ideas“Hard work leads to success.”

Cognitive is what you think, affective what you feel, behavioural what you are ready to do.

Three attitudes matter most at work. Job satisfaction is the positive or negative feeling toward one's job, role and work environment; high satisfaction supports commitment and performance. Organisational commitment is emotional attachment and loyalty to the organisation; strong commitment can reduce turnover and absenteeism. Job involvement is how far a person identifies with their job and treats it as important to their self-worth.

Attitudes are formed by family and early experience, by peer groups and society, by the organisational environment (leadership, rewards, recognition, communication) and by personal experience of success and failure.

text: The Gītā describes three qualities born of nature (sattva, rajas and tamas) that bind every person and mix in different proportions, and later sorts food, work and faith by them. A modern reader may see a trait theory: stable dispositions that shape behaviour. The guṇas are a metaphysical account, not a measured personality test.
pairings.quote: “Sattva, rajas and tamas, the qualities born of nature, bind the embodied self.” सत्त्वं रजस्तम इति गुणाः प्रकृतिसम्भवाः । sattvaṃ rajas tama iti guṇāḥ prakṛti-sambhavāḥ. Bhagavad Gītā 14.5

text: Personality is defined as a relatively consistent pattern. The Gītā observes that even a wise person acts in keeping with their own nature, and that all beings follow theirs: a person's disposition persists from one situation to the next.
pairings.quote: “Even the wise act in keeping with their own nature; beings follow their nature.” सदृशं चेष्टते स्वस्याः प्रकृतेर्ज्ञानवानपि । प्रकृतिं यान्ति भूतानि । sadṛśaṃ ceṣṭate svasyāḥ prakṛter jñānavān api, prakṛtiṃ yānti bhūtāni. Bhagavad Gītā 3.33

text: Tiruvaḷḷuvar's advice for judging people is to look for their merits, then for their faults, and to judge by whichever outweighs the other. It is a direct guard against the halo and horn effects, where one trait decides the whole judgement.
pairings.quote: “Examine a person's merits, examine their faults too, and judge by whichever is greater.” குணம்நாடிக் குற்றமும் நாடி அவற்றுள் மிகைநாடி மிக்க கொளல். Tirukkuṟaḷ 504

pairings.modern: Judging the message by the speaker
text: The Kuṟaḷ defines wisdom as finding the truth of what is said, whoever says it. Judging a message by its source (a respected senior, an unpopular colleague) is a common perceptual error at work.
pairings.quote: “Whatever is heard, from whomever, wisdom is to discern the truth in it.” எப்பொருள் யார்யார்வாய்க் கேட்பினும் அப்பொருள் மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்ப தறிவு. Tirukkuṟaḷ 423

pairings.classic: a person is made of their faith
text: The Gītā says each person's faith takes the shape of their nature, and that a person is made of their faith. Attitude theory makes a narrower claim, a learned tendency to respond in a consistent way, but both see a settled inner stance shaping action.
pairings.quote: “A person is made of their faith: as their faith is, so are they.” श्रद्धामयोऽयं पुरुषो यो यच्छ्रद्धः स एव सः । śraddhāmayo ’yaṃ puruṣo yo yac-chraddhaḥ sa eva saḥ. Bhagavad Gītā 17.3

text: The Dhammapada observes that people see others' faults easily and their own with difficulty, sifting the first like chaff and hiding the second like a gambler hiding a losing throw. That is the asymmetry attribution research later measured: we explain others' failures by their character and our own by circumstance.
pairings.quote: “The faults of others are easy to see, one's own hard to see. One winnows others' faults like chaff, but hides one's own, as a cheat hides a losing throw.” सुदस्सं वज्जमञ्ञेसं । अत्तनो पन दुद्दसं । परेसं हि सो वज्जानि ओपुनाति यथा भुसं । अत्तनो पन छादेति कलिं व कितवा सठो । sudassaṃ vajjam aññesaṃ, attano pana duddasaṃ; paresaṃ hi so vajjāni opunāti yathā bhusaṃ; attano pana chādeti kaliṃ va kitavā saṭho. Dhammapada 252 (Pali)

chapters.title: Values, Learning and Motivation
chapters.scope: What shapes individual behaviour, the values people steer by, how they learn, and what moves them to act.

blocks.title: What shapes individual behaviour
blocks.html:
Individual behaviour is how a person acts, thinks and responds. It is shaped by internal traits, learned experience and surroundings, and understanding it helps explain people's reactions and improve how the organisation works.

FactorWhat it includesAt work
BiologicalAge, gender, health, heredityPhysical and emotional abilities; adaptability and handling of stress may vary.
PsychologicalPersonality, perception, attitude, beliefsAn optimistic employee may see a deadline as a challenge rather than a threat.
EnvironmentalCulture, family, peers, workplaceCollectivist cultures stress teamwork; individualist cultures stress personal success.

blocks.title: Values
blocks.html:
Values are deep beliefs that guide actions and decisions: what a person considers right, desirable or important. They are stable and enduring (often formed early through family and culture), act as standards for judging actions and people, influence ethical behaviour and responsibility, and shape priorities in life and work.

Rokeach's value typesMeaningExamples
Terminal valuesEnd goals a person strives forFreedom, inner harmony, wisdom
Instrumental valuesThe means, or principles, used to reach themHonesty, responsibility, politeness

Terminal values are ends; instrumental values are means.

blocks.title: Learning
blocks.html:
Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour or knowledge that comes from experience, observation or practice. It builds adaptability and competence. It can be active or passive, intentional or unintentional; it is lifelong; and it changes thoughts, attitudes and skills.

TheoryKey ideaExampleAt work
Classical conditioning (Pavlov)Learning by association between a neutral stimulus and a natural responseA school bell comes to signal lunch, and hungerAdvertising links emotions with products
Operant conditioning (Skinner)Behaviour shaped by rewards and punishmentsPraise for an early submission makes it more likely againBonuses encourage performance
Cognitive learning (Tolman, Piaget)Learning through reasoning, thinking and problem-solvingMind maps to understand a topicCase analysis in corporate training
Social learning (Bandura)Learning by observing and imitating othersA new employee copies a punctual seniorRole models shape habits

blocks.title: Motivation
blocks.html:
Motivation is the internal or external push that directs behaviour toward goals. It energises behaviour, guides it and sustains it.

TheoryCore ideaAt work
Maslow's hierarchy of needsNeeds rise from physiological, to safety, to social, to esteem, to self-actualisationMatch benefits and incentives to the needs employees have now
Herzberg's two-factor theoryMotivators create satisfaction; hygiene factors only prevent dissatisfactionPay is a hygiene factor; recognition is a motivator
McClelland's needs theoryBehaviour is driven by the needs for achievement, affiliation and powerAssign work to suit the dominant need
Vroom's expectancy theoryEffort leads to performance, and performance to rewardClear goals and valued rewards strengthen motivation
Motivation = Expectancy × Instrumentality × Valence

text: Manu lists ten marks of dharma: steadiness, forgiveness, self-control, not stealing, purity, restraint of the senses, wisdom, learning, truthfulness and freedom from anger. Most are ways of acting rather than end goals, close to Rokeach's instrumental values such as honesty and responsibility. Manu does not divide ends from means this way, so the comparison is a reading.
pairings.quote: धृतिः क्षमा दमोऽस्तेयं शौचमिन्द्रियनिग्रहः । धीर्विद्या सत्यमक्रोधो दशकं धर्मलक्षणम् । dhṛtiḥ kṣamā damo ’steyaṃ śaucam indriya-nigrahaḥ, dhīr vidyā satyam akrodho daśakaṃ dharma-lakṣaṇam. “Steadiness, forgiveness, self-control, not stealing, purity, restraint of the senses, wisdom, learning, truth and freedom from anger: these ten are the marks of dharma.” Manusmṛti 6.92

text: Patañjali says practice becomes firmly grounded when it is kept up for a long time, without interruption and with care. Learning theory describes the same result, a lasting change through practice, and adds that rewards and observation also shape it.
pairings.quote: “Practice becomes firmly grounded when it is pursued for a long time, without a break, and with devotion.” स तु दीर्घकालनैरन्तर्यसत्कारासेवितो दृढभूमिः । sa tu dīrgha-kāla-nairantarya-satkārāsevito dṛḍha-bhūmiḥ. Yoga Sūtra 1.14

text: Bandura's social learning theory holds that people learn by watching and imitating others. The Gītā observes that people do what the best among them do, and follow the standard those people set.
pairings.quote: “Whatever the best person does, others do too; the world follows the standard they set.” यद्यदाचरति श्रेष्ठस्तत्तदेवेतरो जनः । स यत्प्रमाणं कुरुते लोकस्तदनुवर्तते । yad yad ācarati śreṣṭhas tat tad evetaro janaḥ, sa yat pramāṇaṃ kurute lokas tad anuvartate. Bhagavad Gītā 3.21

text: The Taittirīya Upaniṣad describes the person as five layers, each within the last: food, breath, mind, understanding and bliss. A modern reader may see Maslow's climb from physiological needs to self-actualisation. The Upaniṣad describes the self, not a sequence of needs at work, so the link is a reading.
pairings.quote: “Within it is another self.” अन्योऽन्तर आत्मा । anyo ’ntara ātmā. Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1–2.5

text: The Kuṟaḷ says that effort creates prosperity and the lack of it brings poverty. Vroom's expectancy theory asks whether people believe effort will lead to performance and performance to reward. The couplet states the first link with confidence; the theory treats it as a belief that may be weak.
pairings.quote: “Effort brings prosperity; the absence of effort brings poverty.” முயற்சி திருவினை ஆக்கும் முயற்றின்மை இன்மை புகுத்தி விடும். Tirukkuṟaḷ 616

chapters.title: Group Behaviour, Teams and Leadership
chapters.scope: How people act together: kinds of groups and their norms, how teams develop, how leaders lead, and the forces at work inside a group.

blocks.title: Groups and group norms
blocks.html:
Put five capable people in a room and they behave differently than they would alone: some go quiet, some go along, some ease off. Group behaviour is the study of why.

In plain wordsA group is a few people who deal with each other and need each other to get something done.

Exam definitionA group is two or more individuals, interacting and interdependent, who have come together to achieve particular objectives (Robbins and Judge).

Group behaviour is how individuals act, interact and influence one another within a group, through shared goals, roles, communication and social influence. Belonging to a group can change a person's behaviour, attitudes and decisions.

Formal or informalFormal groupsInformal groups
How they formDeliberately created by the organisationNaturally and spontaneously
BasisStructured roles and assigned tasksShared interests and social relationships
AimSpecific organisational objectivesNot bound by the official structure
ExampleThe finance departmentColleagues who share a lunch table or a cricket team

Group norms are the unwritten rules that guide behaviour and set shared expectations. Positive norms bring harmony and productivity; negative norms bring excessive pressure and lower performance. Example: members mute their phones in meetings without being asked.

Social loafing is putting in less effort in a group than when working alone, on the assumption that others will make up for it. Group performance falls, and so does the motivation of the committed members. Example: two students doing most of a group case study. Maximilien Ringelmann's rope-pulling experiments in the late 1800s first showed it: the more people pulled, the less each pulled. It shrinks when each person's contribution is visible, teams are small, and the task matters to them.

Don't confuse a group with a team. Every team is a group, but not every group is a team. In a team, members share responsibility for one result; in a work group, each answers for their own part.

blocks.title: Team building and Tuckman's stages
blocks.html:
New teams almost always hit a rough patch a few weeks in. Tuckman's stages say that is normal, and show what helps at each point.

Team building is a deliberate process of building trust, collaboration and agreement on goals. It runs from trust, to communication, to resolving conflict, to collaboration, to shared goals. It brings trust and empathy, creativity, better communication and better problem-solving.

Bruce Tuckman described four stages in 1965; with Mary Ann Jensen he added a fifth, adjourning, in 1977. Think of a college fest committee: excited first meetings, a row over the budget, agreed ground rules, a smooth fest weekend, and a farewell dinner.

Tuckman's stageWhat it looks likeWhat helps
1 FormingMembers get acquainted; roles and goals are unclear.Clear goals and roles
2 StormingConflict, personality clashes, the leader challenged.Bring conflict into the open; agree how to work
3 NormingShared norms, roles accepted, trust growing.Reinforce the norms; step back a little
4 PerformingHigh efficiency, synergy, a self-managing team.Delegate, and protect the team from distraction
5 AdjourningThe task is complete; the team disbands and reflects.Recognise the work; record the lessons

Where it breaks. The stages describe a common pattern, not a law. Teams can skip a stage, slip back when a member changes, or storm and perform at the same time.

Forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning.

blocks.title: Leadership
blocks.html:
Two managers take over two branches of the same bank. Same rules, same pay, same kind of customers. A year later one team is steady and the other has lost three people. What differed was how each one led.

In plain wordsLeadership is getting people to want to move in a direction, not only telling them to.

Exam definitionLeadership is the ability to influence a group toward the achievement of a vision or set of goals (Robbins and Judge).

A leader's core roles are to set direction, manage conflict, inspire and improve productivity. Thinking about how to do this has moved through four broad answers.

ApproachThe question it asksKey ideas
Trait (1930s–40s)Who makes a good leader?Drive, integrity, self-confidence, intelligence, knowledge of the business. No list of traits guarantees results.
Behavioural (1940s–60s)What do good leaders do?Lewin's three styles; the Ohio State studies (initiating structure and consideration); the Michigan studies (job-centred and employee-centred); Blake and Mouton's managerial grid
Contingency (1960s–70s)Which style suits which situation?Fiedler's contingency model; Hersey and Blanchard's situational leadership; House's path–goal theory
Transformational (1970s onward)How do leaders change what followers want?Burns's transactional and transformational leadership; Bass's four Is; Greenleaf's servant leadership

Lewin's three styles (1939) are still the starting point:

StyleCore featureBest use and risk
AutocraticThe leader makes decisions aloneCrises and emergencies; fast, but overuse may demoralise
DemocraticMembers take part in decisionsBuilds participation and ownership; decisions may be slower
Laissez-faireHigh autonomy, minimal guidanceSkilled, self-motivated teams

Situational leadership turns the contingency idea into a practical rule: match the style to how ready the follower is for the task.

Transformational leaders change what followers want, not only what they do. Transactional leaders trade reward for effort. Verghese Kurien built Amul around an idea dairy farmers could own: a cooperative run by and for its milk producers. That is the transformational kind.

Effective leaders are visionary (future and strategic direction), empathetic (understand others' feelings), communicative (clear information and ideas), ethical (fair and morally sound decisions) and decisive (confident action).

Don't confuse leadership with management. In John Kotter's distinction, management copes with complexity: plans, budgets, control. Leadership copes with change: direction, alignment, motivation. Most managers need both.

Where it breaks. Style labels describe tendencies, not fixed types; most leaders shift between them. Trait lists read well but predict little on their own. Situational leadership is popular in training, but research gives it only mixed support.

For exams. Match each theory to its author and its key terms: LPC (Fiedler), readiness (Hersey and Blanchard), path–goal (House), the four Is (Bass), the grid (Blake and Mouton).

Go deeper for practitioners

Fiedler's contingency model (1967) treats style as fixed. A leader is task-motivated or relationship-motivated, measured by the least preferred co-worker (LPC) scale. A situation is more or less favourable depending on leader–member relations, task structure and position power. Task-motivated leaders do best when the situation is very favourable or very unfavourable; relationship-motivated leaders in between. The advice is to change the situation, or the leader, rather than the style.

House's path–goal theory (1971) says a leader's job is to clear the path to goals. It names four behaviours: directive, supportive, participative and achievement-oriented, chosen to fit the task and the people.

Blake and Mouton's grid (1964) plots concern for production against concern for people, each from 1 to 9: 1,1 impoverished; 9,1 authority–compliance; 1,9 country club; 5,5 middle of the road; 9,9 team management, the one they recommend.

Bass's four Is of transformational leadership: idealised influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation and individualised consideration. In Judge and Piccolo's 2004 review of many studies, both transformational leadership and contingent reward, a transactional behaviour, were strongly linked with followers' satisfaction and leaders' effectiveness; laissez-faire was linked with worse results.

A decision. A strong performer is promoted to lead her former peers. They are skilled and keen. Situational leadership says delegate; her instinct, wanting to prove herself, is to direct. Which costs more if she gets it wrong?

blocks.title: Group dynamics
blocks.html:
A board of capable people can still make a decision none of them would have made alone. Group dynamics explains how.

Group dynamics are the psychological processes and patterns of interaction at work within a group. They shape participation, collaboration, conflict resolution and performance.

  • Group size. Small groups allow deeper discussion and faster decisions. Large groups bring more diversity, but more coordination and communication problems.
  • Group cohesiveness is the degree of bonding and commitment among members. High cohesiveness improves coordination and performance; extreme cohesiveness may suppress dissent.
  • Groupthink happens when a group values harmony and avoiding conflict above critical evaluation: alternatives are ignored and decisions get worse. Irving Janis built the idea in 1972 from cases such as the Bay of Pigs invasion; Nixon's inner circle during Watergate is also often cited.

Signs of groupthink, in Janis's account: a feeling that the group cannot fail, explaining away warnings, pressure on anyone who disagrees, self-censorship, and an illusion that everyone agrees.

In practice. Ask someone to argue the other side, have the most senior person speak last, and bring in an outsider before a big decision.

Don't confuse cohesion with groupthink. Cohesion helps a group work together. Groupthink is what happens when keeping that cohesion matters more than getting the decision right.

Harmony above critical thinking: alternatives ignored, poor decisions.

text: The Gītā tells Arjuna to do the work that is his, because action is better than inaction. Social loafing is the opposite habit inside a group: holding back because others will cover. The verse speaks to one person's duty, not to group work, so the link is a reading.
pairings.quote: “Do your allotted work, for action is better than inaction.” नियतं कुरु कर्म त्वं कर्म ज्यायो ह्यकर्मणः । niyataṃ kuru karma tvaṃ karma jyāyo hy akarmaṇaḥ. Bhagavad Gītā 3.8

pairings.classic: the crow that calls its kin
text: The Kuṟaḷ notes that a crow does not hide its food but calls its kin to share it, and says prosperity stays with people of that nature. Team building aims at the same habit: members who share rather than hoard. The couplet is about a ruler and his kin, so the comparison is offered for reflection.
pairings.quote: “The crow does not hide its food but calls its kin to eat; prosperity belongs to those of such nature.” காக்கை கரவா கரைந்துண்ணும் ஆக்கமும் அன்னநீ ரார்க்கே உள. Tirukkuṟaḷ 527

text: Tiruvaḷḷuvar names four qualities that should never fail in a ruler: fearlessness, generosity, wisdom and energy. They sit close to the traits listed for effective leaders, such as being decisive and visionary.
pairings.quote: “Fearlessness, generosity, wisdom and energy: never lacking these four is the nature of a ruler.” அஞ்சாமை ஈகை அறிவூக்கம் இந்நான்கும் எஞ்சாமை வேந்தற் கியல்பு. Tirukkuṟaḷ 382

text: The Kuṟaḷ asks who could ruin a ruler who keeps advisers willing to rebuke him. Groupthink is the failure of that check: harmony is valued above critical evaluation, and the objections are never voiced.
pairings.quote: “Who can ruin the ruler who keeps advisers willing to rebuke him?” இடிக்குந் துணையாரை யாள்வாரை யாரே கெடுக்குந் தகைமை யவர். Tirukkuṟaḷ 447

pairings.classic: one who acts as he speaks
text: Tukaram says he will bow to the feet of whoever acts as he speaks. Leadership research finds credibility, doing what you say you will do, at the base of followers' trust. Tukaram is honouring a devotee, not describing a manager, so the link is a reading.
pairings.quote: “Whoever acts as he speaks, I will bow to his feet.” बोले तैसा चाले । त्याचीं वंदीन पाउलें ॥ bole taisā chāle, tyācīṃ vandīn pāuleṃ. Tukārām Gāthā 4291 (Marathi; Wikisource numbering)

chapters.title: Interpersonal Behaviour and Transactional Analysis
chapters.scope: How people communicate and respond to one another, the skills that make it work, and Eric Berne's transactional analysis.

blocks.title: Interpersonal behaviour and its patterns
blocks.html:
Interpersonal behaviour is how people communicate, respond and interact with one another, through verbal and non-verbal communication: tone, body language, emotions and gestures. It shapes teamwork, leadership, conflict resolution and organisational culture.

PatternCore idea
One-to-oneIndividual interaction; trust and clarity matter.
One-to-manyA leader communicates with a group; needs clarity and confidence.
Many-to-oneSeveral employees communicate with a superior; needs active listening.
Many-to-manyTeam interaction; needs collaboration, respect and openness.

Reciprocal influence: A's behaviour influences B, and B's response in turn influences A. Positive behaviour strengthens morale, motivation and cooperation; negative behaviour weakens them.

blocks.title: Types, determinants and skills
blocks.html:
Cooperative behaviour works toward shared goals with respect and openness, and brings teamwork, creativity and collaboration. Conflicting behaviour arises from different goals, perceptions or misunderstandings; managed constructively, it brings role clarity, better understanding and innovative solutions.

Six things determine how people behave toward one another: personality, perception, attitudes, values, emotional intelligence and motivation.

  • Positive thinking builds resilience and encourages constructive responses.
  • Mutual trust promotes transparency and open communication.
  • Empathy is understanding others' emotions and perspectives.
  • Courtesy maintains respect and professional decorum.
  • Avoiding ego clashes supports harmony, cooperation and teamwork.

blocks.title: Transactional analysis: Johari window, ego states and transactions
blocks.html:
Transactional analysis (TA), developed by Eric Berne, explains interactions through ego states, and is used to improve self-awareness, communication and relationships.

Johari window areaKnown to selfKnown to othersWhat to do
OpenYesYesBuild trust and transparency
BlindNoYesReduce through feedback
HiddenYesNoReduce through self-disclosure
UnknownNoNoExplore through experience

The Johari window was developed by Joseph Luft and Harrington Ingham. The goal is to enlarge the open area, for better self-awareness, understanding and trust.

Ego stateWhat it holdsHow it shows
ParentValues, attitudes and behaviour learned from authority figuresGuiding or critical
AdultLogical, factual, rational processingObjective decisions
ChildEmotional, spontaneous, dependent responsesPlayful or rebellious

Transactions: in a complementary transaction the reply comes from the ego state the sender addressed (adult to adult), so communication flows. In a crossed transaction the reply comes from an unexpected ego state, causing misunderstanding or conflict. In an ulterior transaction two messages travel at once: an apparent social one and a hidden psychological one.

blocks.title: Life scripts, life positions, strokes and games
blocks.html:
A life script is a largely unconscious pattern formed in childhood that shapes later decisions, relationships and behaviour. TA aims to recognise unhelpful patterns, change behaviour and support personal growth.

Life positionOrientationResult
I'm OK, you're OKPositive toward self and othersHealthy relationships: the ideal position
I'm OK, you're not OKSuperior, blamingTension and conflict
I'm not OK, you're OKInferior, submissiveDependency
I'm not OK, you're not OKNegative toward self and othersDisengagement

A stroke is an act of recognition. Positive strokes (praise, appreciation) build morale and motivation; negative strokes (criticism, disapproval) may discourage. Managers should give genuine, constructive recognition.

Games are recurring patterns of interaction with hidden motives that lead to predictable, often unhelpful outcomes. In “Yes, but…”, a person asks for solutions and then rejects each one, avoiding responsibility.

text: The Kuṟaḷ says friendship is not for laughing together but for stepping in to rebuke a friend who goes wrong. In Johari's terms, a friend's honest feedback shrinks the blind area: what others can see in us that we cannot.
pairings.quote: “Friendship is not for laughing together; it is for stepping in to rebuke when one goes too far.” நகுதற் பொருட்டன்று நட்டல் மிகுதிக்கண் மேற்சென் றிடித்தற் பொருட்டு. Tirukkuṟaḷ 784

text: The Kaṭha Upaniṣad pictures the self as a rider in a chariot: the body is the chariot, the intellect the charioteer and the mind the reins. A modern reader may see the Adult ego state as the charioteer, steering learned habit and raw feeling. The Upaniṣad describes the self's journey, so this is a reading, not Berne's model.
pairings.quote: “Know the self as the rider, the body as the chariot, the intellect as the charioteer and the mind as the reins.” आत्मानं रथिनं विद्धि शरीरं रथमेव तु । बुद्धिं तु सारथिं विद्धि मनः प्रग्रहमेव च । ātmānaṃ rathinaṃ viddhi śarīraṃ ratham eva tu, buddhiṃ tu sārathiṃ viddhi manaḥ pragraham eva ca. Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.3

text: Kabir advises keeping a critic close, even housing him in your courtyard, because he cleans your nature without soap or water. The Johari window says the blind area, what others see in us and we do not, shrinks only through feedback. Both treat criticism from others as the way to see yourself.
pairings.quote: “Keep your critic close; give him a hut in your courtyard. Without water, without soap, he makes your nature clean.” निन्दक नियरे राखिये, आंगन कुटी छवाय । बिन पानी साबुन बिना, निरमल करे सुभाय ॥ nindak niyare rākhiye, āṅgan kuṭī chhavāy; bin pānī sābun binā, nirmal kare subhāy. Kabīr, sākhī (Hindi)

chapters.title: Organisational Culture and Climate
chapters.scope: The shared meaning that makes one organisation unlike another, how it is built and kept, and how it feels to work there.

blocks.title: What organisational culture is
blocks.html:
Organisational culture is a system of shared meaning held by members that distinguishes one organisation from another: the shared values, beliefs and norms that shape how things are done there.

DimensionWhat it measures
Innovation and risk-takingExperimentation, creativity, willingness to take risks
Attention to detailPrecision, analysis, thoroughness
Outcome orientationResults, performance, achieving targets
People orientationThe effect of decisions on employees and their well-being
Team orientationCollaboration and collective achievement
AggressivenessCompetitiveness and assertiveness
StabilityOrder, consistency, keeping the status quo

blocks.title: Strength and functions of culture
blocks.html:
A dominant culture is the core values most members accept, often shaped by founders and top management. Subcultures are smaller cultures within departments, locations or professions that combine the organisation's values with local experience.

Strong cultureWeak culture
Looks likeShared beliefs, clear norms, common goalsFragmented beliefs, inconsistent messages
Leads toLoyalty, engagement and consistent behaviourLess unity, weaker values, disconnected employees
FunctionWhat culture does
Boundary definitionDistinguishes the organisation from others
IdentityGives members a sense of belonging
CommitmentConnects employees to a shared mission
StabilityActs as social glue holding the organisation together
Behaviour guideSignals what is acceptable, even without formal rules

blocks.title: How culture is built and kept
blocks.html:
Culture starts with the founder's philosophy, whose values shape hiring, leadership style and expectations. Top management keeps it alive as role models through their decisions and behaviour. Reinforcement mechanisms strengthen it: selection, training, performance evaluation, rewards and promotion.

Socialisation stageWhat happens
Pre-arrivalExpectations form before joining, through interviews, websites and reviews.
EncounterExpectations meet reality through orientation, onboarding and practice.
MetamorphosisThe employee adapts and fits into the organisation's norms.

A positive culture builds on employees' strengths rather than dwelling on weaknesses, rewards more than it punishes, and supports growth through learning, creativity and career development. Its limit: positivity does not remove the need for objective standards and constructive feedback.

blocks.title: Types of culture, and climate
blocks.html:
TypeCharacterValues
Clan (collaborate)Warm, family-likeMentoring, teamwork, involvement
Adhocracy (create)Dynamic, entrepreneurialInnovation, risk-taking, adaptability
Market (compete)Competitive, results-drivenGoals, performance, measurable outcomes
Hierarchy (control)Structured, rule-basedStability, order, formal procedures

Organisational climate is the shared perception members have of their organisation and work environment. Climate can be people-oriented (well-being and morale), rule-oriented (policies and procedures), innovation-oriented (creativity and new ideas) or goal-oriented (targets and performance).

CultureClimate
FocusShared values and meaningsShared perceptions and feelings
NatureDeep-rooted, relatively stableMore immediate and changeable
TimeLong-termCurrent experience
Core question“How do we do things here?”“What does it feel like to work here?”

Culture is values and meaning; climate is perceptions and feelings.

text: Kauṭilya opens his chapter on the ruler's duties by observing that when the ruler is active his servants become active too, and when he is careless they grow careless and eat into his work. Culture theory says the same of founders and top managers: their conduct becomes the standard.
pairings.quote: “When the ruler is active, his servants rise with him; when he is careless, they are careless too.” राजानमुत्थितमनूत्तिष्ठन्ते भृत्याः । प्रमाद्यन्तमनुप्रमाद्यन्ति । rājānam utthitam anūttiṣṭhante bhṛtyāḥ; pramādyantam anupramādyanti. Arthaśāstra 1.19.1–2

pairings.classic: where the mind is without fear
text: Tagore's poem asks for a place where the mind is without fear, the head held high and knowledge free. A people-oriented or innovation-oriented climate rests on the same conditions: people speak up when they are not afraid, and ideas move when knowledge is shared. Tagore was praying for a country, so the comparison is a reading.
pairings.quote: “Where the mind is without fear and the head is held high; where knowledge is free.” চিত্ত যেথা ভয়শূন্য, উচ্চ যেথা শির, জ্ঞান যেথা মুক্ত chitto jetha bhoyshunyo, uchcho jetha shir, gyan jetha mukto Rabindranath Tagore, Naivedya 72 (Bengali, 1901); his English in Gitanjali 35

chapters.title: Workforce Diversity and Cross-Cultural Behaviour
chapters.scope: Recognising and respecting differences at work, managing them fairly, and working well across national cultures.

blocks.title: Workforce diversity and its dimensions
blocks.html:
Workforce diversity is recognising and respecting differences among employees in age, gender, race, religion, ethnicity, physical ability and background. Diversity is more than tolerance: it means inclusion, equal opportunity and respect. Its benefits include innovation, creativity, balanced decisions, harmony and efficiency.

Managing diversity means creating a workplace where everyone can perform fairly and without bias, through fairness and equity (equal opportunity), inclusion (valuing different identities), respect (preventing discrimination and exclusion) and a business link (performance and competitiveness).

DimensionWhat it calls for
Race and ethnicityRespect for cultural heritage and traditions; equality at work
Age and generationUnderstanding different values, expectations and ways of communicating
Gender and identityInclusion of all gender identities
Sexual orientationA safe, discrimination-free environment and equal rights
Religious beliefsFlexible schedules, attire and prayer facilities
DisabilityAssistive tools, accessibility and ability-focused roles
Socioeconomic backgroundDiverse perspectives and equal opportunity

blocks.title: Techniques for managing diversity
blocks.html:
TechniqueHow
Raising awarenessTraining, storytelling, discussion
Shared cultureCross-cultural collaboration
Special care programmesFlexible work, accessibility, wellness
Career developmentMentoring, training, promotion
Ending discriminationAddressing hidden bias and the glass ceiling
Preventing sexual harassmentZero tolerance and safe reporting
Diverse committeesSeveral perspectives in decisions

Diversity also plays out in groups: formal groups (organisational tasks, such as an HR team), informal groups (personal relationships, such as a lunch group), and in-groups and out-groups, which create belonging for some and exclusion for others. Members take task roles (the planner), relationship roles (the motivator) or individual roles (the dominator).

blocks.title: Cross-cultural behaviour and Hofstede
blocks.html:
Cross-cultural organisational behaviour studies how cultural differences affect behaviour in multicultural workplaces. Globalisation brings multicultural workplaces and cultural differences, and with them the need to adapt. Done well, it brings adaptation to cultural norms, better international HR strategies, better cooperation, fewer misunderstandings and greater global competitiveness.

Hofstede's dimensionHighLow
Power distanceHierarchy and authority acceptedEquality and informality
Uncertainty avoidanceStructure and risk avoidance (France)Flexibility and openness (Singapore)
Individualism and collectivismSelf-reliance (the United States)Group orientation (India)
Masculinity and femininityCompetition and assertiveness (Japan)Cooperation and quality of life (Sweden)
Time orientationLong-term persistence (China)Short-term results (the United States)

P, U, I, M, T: power distance, uncertainty avoidance, individualism, masculinity, time orientation.

blocks.title: Culture shock and cross-cultural training
blocks.html:
Culture shock is the set of difficulties a person faces in adapting to an unfamiliar culture. Its causes include language barriers, new customs and emotional stress. It is reduced by training, then adjustment support, then integration.

Training areaAim
Self-awarenessUnderstand one's own cultural assumptions
Host-country knowledgeCustoms and workplace practices
Role clarificationResponsibilities and expectations
Intercultural communicationEffective communication across cultures
Conflict resolutionHandling cultural misunderstandings

text: A Ṛgvedic hymn says that what is real is one, and the wise speak of it in many ways. Read for the workplace, it treats differences of expression as compatible with a shared core, the premise of inclusion rather than mere tolerance. The hymn is about naming the divine, so the link is a reading.
pairings.quote: “Truth is one; the wise call it by many names.” एकं सद्विप्रा बहुधा वदन्ति । ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanti. Ṛgveda 1.164.46

text: A verse found in the Mahā Upaniṣad, with a close variant in the Hitopadeśa and the Pañcatantra, says that only the narrow-minded count people as kin and not kin; for the large-hearted, the whole world is one family. In-groups and out-groups are exactly that counting.
pairings.quote: “‘This one is kin, that one is not’ is the reckoning of the small-minded; for those of noble conduct, the whole earth is a family.” अयं बन्धुरयं नेति गणना लघुचेतसाम् । उदारचरितानां तु वसुधैव कुटुम्बकम् । ayaṃ bandhur ayaṃ neti gaṇanā laghucetasām, udāracaritānāṃ tu vasudhaiva kuṭumbakam. Mahā Upaniṣad 6.71

pairings.classic: the customs of regions and guilds
text: Manu tells the ruler, in settling matters, to take account of the customs of castes, of regions, of guilds and of families. Guilds (śreṇī) were the trade associations of the time, so this is an early instruction to recognise each group's own norms and give effect to them, which is what cross-cultural management asks.
pairings.quote: जातिजानपदान्धर्मान्श्रेणीधर्मांश्च धर्मवित् । समीक्ष्य कुलधर्मांश्च स्वधर्मं प्रतिपादयेत् । jāti-jānapadān dharmān śreṇī-dharmāṃś ca dharmavit, samīkṣya kula-dharmāṃś ca sva-dharmaṃ pratipādayet. “One who knows the law should examine the customs of castes, regions, guilds and families, and then establish the law particular to each.” Manusmṛti 8.41

pairings.classic: one caste, one religion, one God
text: Narayana Guru's best-known saying, one caste, one religion, one God for humankind, was a challenge to caste division in Kerala. Diversity management also rejects exclusion, but it goes about it differently: it names differences in order to respect them, where the Guru said the dividing lines had no basis.
pairings.quote: “One caste, one religion, one God for humankind.” ഒരു ജാതി, ഒരു മതം, ഒരു ദൈവം മനുഷ്യന് oru jāti, oru matam, oru daivam manuṣyanŭ. Śrī Nārāyaṇa Guru (Malayalam)

chapters.title: Emotions and Stress Management
chapters.scope: Emotions, moods and emotional intelligence at work, and the causes, effects and management of work stress.

blocks.title: Emotions, moods and affect
blocks.html:
Affect is the broad emotional background of positive and negative feelings: a person's overall emotional tone. Emotions are brief, intense and specific feelings directed at a person or event, such as joy, anger or fear; they trigger quick reactions and influence motivation and decisions. Moods are general, longer-lasting states, often without a definite cause, that colour perception and behaviour over time.

NatureDurationTrigger
EmotionSpecific, intenseShortA particular event or person
MoodGeneral, mildLongOften unknown
AffectBroad emotional toneVariesOverall emotional state

Emotions drive behaviour, influence decisions, prepare the body for action and shape how we read social situations. They may be universal, but display rules vary across cultures, and understanding the differences reduces misunderstanding at work. Six emotions are widely treated as universal: happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise and disgust. Descartes named six primitive passions: wonder, love, hatred, desire, joy and sadness.

blocks.title: Sources of emotions and moods
blocks.html:
SourceEffect
PersonalitySets baseline emotional tendencies.
WeatherEffects are generally limited; a link people perceive may be an illusion of correlation.
StressPersistent demands without relief can trigger negative emotions.
Social interactionPositive contact can lift mood; isolation or conflict may lower it.
SleepPoor sleep weakens emotional regulation: irritability and poorer judgement.
ExerciseHelps improve mood and reduce tension.
AgeEmotional regulation may improve with age and experience.
SexPatterns of expression may differ between men and women, but individual and cultural variation is substantial.

blocks.title: Emotional labour and emotional intelligence
blocks.html:
Emotional labour is managing and displaying the emotions a job requires, which may differ from what the employee actually feels; a customer-service employee stays cheerful while feeling stressed. Emotional dissonance is the gap between felt and displayed emotion. Prolonged, it can lead to fatigue, burnout and job dissatisfaction. Empathy and emotional awareness help manage these demands.

Emotional intelligence (EI) is the ability to recognise, understand and manage one's own emotions and those of others.

ComponentWhat it does
Self-awarenessRecognise your own emotions
Emotional regulationManage your emotional responses
EmpathyUnderstand others
RelationshipsImprove interaction and teamwork

People with high EI tend to stay calm under stress, manage conflict, stay motivated and optimistic, make balanced decisions and work well in teams.

blocks.title: Work stress
blocks.html:
Stress occurs when important demands stretch a person's capacity to cope. Common triggers are excessive pressure, unclear roles and an imbalance between demands and resources: when resources match or exceed demands, stress is lower; when demands exceed resources, the result is strain.

Challenge stressors (deadlines, demanding projects) can energise and motivate. Hindrance stressors (bureaucracy, workplace conflict) get in the way of goals.

SourceExamples
EnvironmentalPolitical instability, economic uncertainty, technological change
OrganisationalHeavy workload, poor management, role ambiguity, conflict
PersonalFamily or financial problems, personality, perfectionism

Small stressors accumulate and can become overwhelming. The consequences are physiological (raised heart rate, headaches, fatigue), psychological (anxiety, mood changes, depression, low satisfaction) and behavioural (absenteeism, lower performance, withdrawal, substance abuse).

Moderate stress may enhance performance; chronic stress brings burnout, illness and decline.

blocks.title: Stress management
blocks.html:
Stress is managed from two sides at once.

Individual approachesOrganisational approaches
Time management: prioritise, organise, cut distractionsSelection and job fit: match skills with roles
Physical exercise: relieve tension, improve energyTraining and development: build competence, reduce anxiety
Relaxation: meditation, deep breathing, mindfulnessClear goal setting: specific goals and feedback
Social support: emotional comfort, advice, copingJob redesign, empowerment and better communication
Sabbaticals and wellness programmes

text: The Gītā's portrait of a person of steady wisdom: undisturbed in sorrow, without craving in pleasure, free of attachment, fear and anger. Emotional regulation aims at a similar steadiness, though emotional intelligence also values recognising emotions, not only rising above them.
pairings.quote: “Undisturbed in sorrow, free of craving in pleasure, without attachment, fear or anger: such a person is called steady in wisdom.” दुःखेष्वनुद्विग्नमनाः सुखेषु विगतस्पृहः । वीतरागभयक्रोधः स्थितधीर्मुनिरुच्यते । duḥkheṣv anudvigna-manāḥ sukheṣu vigata-spṛhaḥ, vīta-rāga-bhaya-krodhaḥ sthita-dhīr munir ucyate. Bhagavad Gītā 2.56

pairings.classic: seeing others' joy and sorrow as one's own
text: The Gītā praises the person who, measuring by themselves, sees the joy and sorrow of others as equal to their own. That is empathy, one of the four parts of emotional intelligence.
pairings.quote: “Who, by comparison with themself, sees the joy and sorrow of all beings as their own is held to be the highest yogin.” आत्मौपम्येन सर्वत्र समं पश्यति योऽर्जुन । सुखं वा यदि वा दुःखं स योगी परमो मतः । ātmaupamyena sarvatra samaṃ paśyati yo ’rjuna, sukhaṃ vā yadi vā duḥkhaṃ sa yogī paramo mataḥ. Bhagavad Gītā 6.32

text: The Kuṟaḷ says the best course is to bear with those who scorn you, as the earth bears those who dig into it. Emotional labour asks something similar of a service employee facing a rude customer. The modern view adds a warning the couplet does not give: a long gap between what is felt and what is shown leads to burnout.
pairings.quote: “As the earth bears those who dig into it, so to bear with those who scorn you is best.” அகழ்வாரைத் தாங்கும் நிலம்போலத் தம்மை இகழ்வார்ப் பொறுத்தல் தலை. Tirukkuṟaḷ 151

pairings.classic: moderation in food, rest and sleep
text: The Gītā says discipline removes sorrow for one who is moderate in eating and recreation, measured in effort at work, and regular in sleep and waking. Exercise, rest and time management, the individual approaches to stress, are that same moderation.
pairings.quote: “For one moderate in food and recreation, measured in effort at work, and regular in sleep and waking, discipline destroys sorrow.” युक्ताहारविहारस्य युक्तचेष्टस्य कर्मसु । युक्तस्वप्नावबोधस्य योगो भवति दुःखहा । yuktāhāra-vihārasya yukta-ceṣṭasya karmasu, yukta-svapnāvabodhasya yogo bhavati duḥkha-hā. Bhagavad Gītā 6.17

text: Śāntideva gives a two-line test for distress: if something can be remedied, dismay is unnecessary; if it cannot, dismay does not help. That is the split stress research makes between problem-focused coping, acting on what can be changed, and managing one's response to what cannot.
pairings.quote: “If there is a remedy, what use is dismay? And if there is no remedy, what use is dismay?” यद्यस्त्येव प्रतीकारो दौर्मनस्येन तत्र किम् । अथ नास्ति प्रतीकारो दौर्मनस्येन तत्र किम् । yady asty eva pratīkāro daurmanasyena tatra kim, atha nāsti pratīkāro daurmanasyena tatra kim. གལ་ཏེ་བཅོས་སུ་ཡོད་ན་ནི། །དེ་ལ་མི་དགར་ཅི་ཞིག་ཡོད། །གལ་ཏེ་བཅོས་སུ་མེད་ན་ནི། །དེ་ལ་མི་དགའ་བྱས་ཅི་ཕན། ། gal te bcos su yod na ni, de la mi dgar ci zhig yod, gal te bcos su med na ni, de la mi dga' byas ci phan. Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra 6.10 (Sanskrit; Tibetan in the Derge Tengyur, Toh 3871)

chapters.title: Organisational Justice and Whistleblowing
chapters.scope: Whether people see their workplace as fair in outcomes, processes and treatment, and how wrongdoing can be reported safely.

blocks.title: Organisational justice
blocks.html:
Organisational justice is employees' perception of fairness in the workplace. It covers both the outcome a person receives and how that outcome is reached and communicated. The term was popularised by Jerald Greenberg (1987).

It matters because fairness builds trust, trust builds morale, morale builds productivity, and all of it helps retain people.

DimensionThe question it asks
DistributiveWas the outcome fair?
ProceduralWas the process fair?
InteractionalWas I treated fairly?

blocks.title: Distributive and procedural justice
blocks.html:
Distributive justice is the perceived fairness of how outcomes are shared out: pay, promotions, recognition, workloads and resources. Three principles can govern the sharing.

PrincipleRewards are based on
EquityContribution or input
EqualityAn equal share for everyone
NeedIndividual needs

Procedural justice is the fairness of the methods used to reach decisions, even when the outcome is unfavourable. It has six requirements: consistency (the same rules for everyone), freedom from bias (no prejudice or favouritism), accuracy (reliable, adequate information), representation (employees have a voice), correctability (a way to challenge or appeal) and ethicality (moral and legal standards upheld).

C, B, A, R, C, E: consistency, bias-free, accuracy, representation, correctability, ethicality.

blocks.title: Interactional justice
blocks.html:
Interactional justice is about how people are treated and how decisions are communicated. It has two parts: interpersonal justice (dignity, respect and courtesy) and informational justice (explanations that are honest, timely and adequate).

Kind of justiceConcerns
DistributiveThe outcome
ProceduralThe process
InteractionalThe treatment

blocks.title: Whistleblowing
blocks.html:
Whistleblowing is reporting organisational wrongdoing to protect ethical, legal and public interests. Common concerns are fraud, financial manipulation, bribery and corruption, unsafe conditions, discrimination, insider trading and other unethical acts.

Employees, customers and clients, contractors, consultants, vendors and suppliers may all report. Whistleblowers risk retaliation: career setbacks, legal threats, social ostracism and harassment.

Internal whistleblowingExternal whistleblowing
Reported toHR, senior management, an ethics committeeRegulators, legal authorities, the media
WhenGenerally the preferred first step, giving the organisation a chance to actWhen internal mechanisms fail or the environment is hostile

Wrongdoing, then internal reporting, then resolution; if unresolved or hostile, external reporting.

blocks.title: Reportable offences, benefits and India's framework
blocks.html:
Reportable offences include legal, contractual and ethical violations, financial or data fraud, health and safety risks, environmental violations, misuse of property or funds, abuse of power and intellectual property violations.

For the organisation, whistleblowing brings early detection of legal and operational risks, trust among employees, customers and investors, an ethical culture, a responsible public image, prevention of major scandals, and transparency.

IndiaWhat it provides
Companies Act, 2013Mechanisms for inspecting a company's affairs; the Serious Fraud Investigation Office for serious fraud; vigil mechanisms required of specified companies.
SEBI frameworkWhistleblower mechanisms in listed entities, with avenues and safeguards for reporting.
Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014A framework for receiving public-interest disclosures about corruption or misuse of power by public servants, and for protecting those who make them against victimisation. Enacted, but not yet brought into force.

False or malicious complaints may attract penalties under the applicable law.

text: The Kuṟaḷ calls it the ornament of the wise to be like a balance that weighs evenly and leans to neither side. Organisational justice is that impartiality, as employees perceive it.
pairings.quote: “Like a balance that weighs evenly, leaning to neither side: such impartiality is the ornament of the wise.” சமன்செய்து சீர்தூக்குங் கோல்போல் அமைந்தொருபால் கோடாமை சான்றோர்க் கணி. Tirukkuṟaḷ 118

text: The Kuṟaḷ says that when a ruler does not treat everyone alike but regards each according to their worth, many will live by that regard. Distributive justice by equity, reward in line with contribution, is the same principle.
pairings.quote: “If the ruler does not regard all alike but each by their worth, many will live by that regard.” பொதுநோக்கான் வேந்தன் வரிசையா நோக்கின் அதுநோக்கி வாழ்வார் பலர். Tirukkuṟaḷ 528

text: Justice, says the Kuṟaḷ, is to examine carefully, show favour to no one, and act impartially toward all after weighing the matter. Procedural justice sets out the same requirements: accuracy, freedom from bias and consistency.
pairings.quote: “To inquire, to favour none, to act impartially toward all after weighing the matter: that is justice.” ஓர்ந்துகண் ணோடா திறைபுரிந் தியார்மாட்டும் தேர்ந்துசெய் வஃதே முறை. Tirukkuṟaḷ 541

text: The Kuṟaḷ compares speaking harshly when kind words are at hand to picking unripe fruit when ripe fruit is there. Interactional justice asks that decisions, even hard ones, be delivered with dignity, respect and courtesy.
pairings.quote: “To speak harshly when kind words are at hand is to pick the unripe fruit when the ripe is there.” இனிய உளவாக இன்னாத கூறல் கனியிருப்பக் காய்கவர்ந் தற்று. Tirukkuṟaḷ 100

pairings.classic: a ruler who can be reached
text: Kauṭilya warns the ruler not to keep people with business waiting at his door: a ruler who is hard to reach is made, by those around him, to confuse what should and should not be done. Internal reporting channels serve a similar purpose in a company, a way for bad news to reach the top past the inner circle. Kauṭilya is writing about petitions to a king, so the link is a reading.
pairings.quote: Arthaśāstra 1.19

pairings.classic: do not despise, do not belittle
text: Basavanna's vacana lists what not to do: steal, kill, lie, rage, despise others, praise yourself, belittle the person in front of you, and calls this purity inside and out. Interpersonal justice asks for dignity, respect and courtesy in how people are treated. The vacana is a personal code, so the link is a reading.
pairings.quote: “Do not steal, do not kill, do not lie, do not rage, do not despise others, do not praise yourself, do not belittle the one before you. This is inner purity; this is outer purity.” ಕಳಬೇಡ, ಕೊಲಬೇಡ, ಹುಸಿಯ ನುಡಿಯಲು ಬೇಡ, ಮುನಿಯ ಬೇಡ, ಅನ್ಯರಿಗೆ ಅಸಹ್ಯಪಡಬೇಡ, ತನ್ನ ಬಣ್ಣಿಸಬೇಡ, ಇದಿರ ಹಳಿಯಲು ಬೇಡ. ಇದೇ ಅಂತರಂಗಶುದ್ಧಿ, ಇದೇ ಬಹಿರಂಗಶುದ್ಧಿ. kaḷabēḍa, kolabēḍa, husiya nuḍiyalu bēḍa, muniya bēḍa, anyarige asahyapaḍabēḍa, tanna baṇṇisabēḍa, idira haḷiyalu bēḍa. idē antaraṅgaśuddhi, idē bahiraṅgaśuddhi. Basavaṇṇa, vacana (Kannada)

chapters.title: Human Resource Management
chapters.scope: What HRM is, how it grew, what it aims at and does, and how it differs from personnel management and from organisational behaviour.

blocks.title: Meaning and objectives of HRM
blocks.html:
Human resource management (HRM) is the process of acquiring, developing, motivating and retaining employees to achieve organisational goals. It aims to maximise performance, ensure employee welfare and align people with the organisation's strategy.

Acquire → Develop → Motivate → Retain: a skilled, motivated and committed workforce
ObjectivesExamples
PersonalTraining, career development, work-life balance, satisfaction
OrganisationalProductivity, performance, workforce planning, talent management
OtherLegal compliance, social responsibility, diversity and inclusion, fairness

blocks.title: Evolution of HRM
blocks.html:
StagePeriodFocus
Pre-industrialBefore the 18th centuryAgrarian and manual work; no formal HR
Industrial Revolution18th–19th centuryFactory system, supervision, discipline, productivity
Scientific managementLate 19th–early 20th centuryF. W. Taylor: efficiency, time and motion, standardisation
Human relations1920s–1930sElton Mayo: social factors, morale, motivation
Post-war personnel1940s–1950sPersonnel departments, hiring, training, labour relations
Modern HRM1960s–1980sFrom personnel administration to HR development and motivation
TQM and globalisation1980s–1990sQuality, employee involvement, continuous improvement
Strategic HRM2000s onwardHR information systems, analytics, diversity, a global workforce, strategic alignment

Control, efficiency, human relations, personnel, HRM, strategic HR.

blocks.title: Functions of HRM
blocks.html:
FunctionActivityPurpose
PlanHuman resource planningForecast manpower requirements
AcquireRecruitment and selectionAttract and select suitable employees
DevelopTraining and developmentBuild knowledge, skills and capabilities
EvaluatePerformance appraisalAssess performance and find areas to improve
RewardCompensation managementFair pay, benefits and retention
RelateEmployee relationsCommunication, cooperation and conflict resolution
ProtectSafety and welfareHealth, safety and well-being
PrepareCareer and succession planningFuture talent and leadership continuity

blocks.title: Approaches to HRM, and how HRM differs
blocks.html:
ApproachCore idea
TraditionalAdministrative control, records, compliance
Human relationsMotivation, morale and social needs
Human resource developmentLearning, skills and career development
ContingencyHR practices depend on the situation; no single best way
Strategic HRMHR strategy aligned with business strategy
High-performance work systemsTeamwork, empowerment and performance-linked rewards
Best practicesSome HR practices improve performance almost everywhere
Resource-based viewPeople as strategic resources for lasting competitive advantage
Employee-centricWell-being, engagement, flexibility and inclusion
Evidence-basedData and evidence guide HR decisions
HRMPersonnel management
PhilosophyStrategic and proactiveAdministrative and reactive
FocusPeople and business strategyRoutine employee administration
ScopeBroad: development, engagement, planningNarrow: payroll, records, compliance
Employee relationsParticipation and engagementControl and grievance handling
DevelopmentLearning, potential and growthMainly task-specific training

HRM asks “How do we manage people?”; organisational behaviour asks “Why do people behave the way they do?”

text: The Kuṟaḷ's rule for assigning work: having judged that this person will accomplish this task by these means, leave the task to them. Acquiring and developing a workforce turns that judgement into a system.
pairings.quote: “Having judged that this person can accomplish this task by these means, entrust the task to them.” இதனை இதனால் இவன்முடிக்கும் என்றாய்ந் ததனை அவன்கண் விடல். Tirukkuṟaḷ 517

chapters.title: Human Resource Planning
chapters.scope: Forecasting and balancing the demand for and supply of people, so the right people are in the right place at the right time.

blocks.title: Meaning of human resource planning
blocks.html:
Human resource planning (HRP) is the process of forecasting and managing the demand for and supply of human resources. It makes sure the organisation has the right people, in the right place, at the right time.

Its core objective is balance: between the human resources available and what the organisation requires.

blocks.title: The HRP process
blocks.html:
StepWhat it involves
1 Analyse organisational objectivesUnderstand the mission, strategy and future business goals
2 Forecast HR demandEstimate future workforce needs from expansion, technology and production
3 Analyse HR supplyAssess available talent, skills, turnover, promotions and succession
4 Identify skill gapsCompare existing skills with those required
5 Determine workforce requirementsThe number and type of employees needed, by department
6 Match demand and supplyFind shortages or surpluses
7 Develop HR action plansRecruitment, training, redeployment, retention
8 Monitor and controlTrack measures, review outcomes, update plans as conditions change

Strategy, forecast, analyse, match, act, review.

blocks.title: Methods of supply analysis
blocks.html:
MethodLooks at
Skills inventoryEmployees' qualifications, skills and experience
Succession planningPotential future leaders for critical positions
Turnover analysisExit patterns and what they mean for future staffing
Promotion and mobility analysisInternal movement and advancement potential
Job analysisDuties, responsibilities and required competencies
Scenario planningPossible future situations and their workforce implications

pairings.modern: Right person, right work, right time
pairings.classic: the doer, the work and the time
text: The Kuṟaḷ advises acting only after weighing the doer, the work and the right time together. Human resource planning asks a workforce the same three questions: who, for what work, and when.
pairings.quote: “Weigh the doer, weigh the work, and act knowing the right time.” செய்வானை நாடி வினைநாடிக் காலத்தோடு எய்த உணர்ந்து செயல். Tirukkuṟaḷ 516

chapters.title: Recruitment and Selection
chapters.scope: Attracting a pool of suitable candidates, then choosing the best of them: the sources, the steps and the tests.

blocks.title: Recruitment and its sources
blocks.html:
Recruitment is the process of searching for, identifying and attracting qualified candidates for job vacancies. Its purpose is to build a pool of capable candidates for current and future needs: from a vacancy, to attracting candidates, to a talent pool, to selection.

Internal methodKey focus
Job postingAnnouncing the vacancy internally
Employee referralsRecommendations by employees
PromotionsMovement to higher positions
TransfersMovement across departments or locations
Rehiring retired employeesPart-time or project engagement
Previous applicantsReconsidering earlier applicants

Internal recruitment costs less, is faster, lifts morale and supports career development. External recruitment brings a wider talent pool, fresh skills, new perspectives and innovation. Its sources include online recruitment, social media, recruitment agencies, job fairs, campus recruitment, headhunting, internships, walk-ins, temporary or contract hiring, poaching and government job centres.

blocks.title: The recruitment process
blocks.html:
StepPurpose
1 Identify the vacancyRecognise the staffing need
2 Job analysisDetermine duties and required skills
3 Job description and specificationDefine responsibilities and qualifications
4 Advertise the jobUse internal and external channels
5 Receive and review applicationsScreen and shortlist
6 Build a talent poolKeep potential candidates in view
7 Employer brandingAttract quality applicants
8 Initial communicationGive role clarity
9 NetworkingReach passive candidates
10 Recruitment campaignsPlan hiring drives
11 Tracking and reportingEvaluate how well recruitment worked

Need, analyse, attract, screen, build, evaluate.

blocks.title: Selection and selection tests
blocks.html:
Selection is the process of evaluating and choosing the most suitable candidate from the applicant pool. Its goal is to match the candidate's skills, attitude and values with the organisation's requirements.

Application review → preliminary screening → shortlisting → interview → tests → verification → medical → offer → onboarding
Selection testMeasures
Intelligence testReasoning, analysis and problem-solving
Aptitude testAbility to learn job-specific skills
Interest testOccupational preferences
Personality testBehaviour and emotional stability
Achievement testJob-related knowledge and proficiency
Trade testTechnical, job-specific ability
Dexterity testManual skill and coordination

blocks.title: Recruitment against selection
blocks.html:
RecruitmentSelection
MeaningAttracting potential candidatesChoosing the best candidate
ObjectiveCreate an applicant poolIdentify the suitable candidate
NaturePositive: encourages applicantsNegative: eliminates unsuitable applicants
ScopeBroad: sourcing and attractingNarrow: screening and evaluation
OutcomeA pool of candidatesThe final hiring decision
ResponsibilityMainly the HR recruitment teamHR with departmental heads

Recruitment attracts, for more candidates; selection chooses, for the best candidate.

text: The Kuṟaḷ says a person should be chosen after being tested on four things: virtue, wealth, pleasure and the fear of losing life. Modern selection tests ability, aptitude and personality; the couplet tests character under temptation and threat.
pairings.quote: “Choose a person after testing them in four ways: by virtue, by wealth, by pleasure and by the fear of death.” அறம்பொருள் இன்பம் உயிரச்சம் நான்கின் திறந்தெரிந்து தேறப் படும். Tirukkuṟaḷ 501

text: Kauṭilya tells the ruler to test ministers in secret through four trials (upadhā), of righteousness, wealth, desire and fear, and to place each in work that suits what the trials showed. The home page's sample concept compares this with modern selection; secret trials of this kind would breach today's ethics and employment law.
pairings.quote: Arthaśāstra 1.10

text: The Kuṟaḷ warns that trusting someone who has not been tested, and doubting someone who has, both bring endless trouble. It is the case for a careful selection process, and for trusting its result once it is done.
pairings.quote: “To trust the untested, and to doubt the one you have tested, both bring endless sorrow.” தேரான் தெளிவும் தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவும் தீரா இடும்பை தரும். Tirukkuṟaḷ 510

text: Vemana notes that salt and camphor look alike, and only tasting shows the difference; so too among people. Selection tests exist for the same reason: applicants who look alike on paper differ once their abilities are tried. Vemana is speaking of character in general, so this is a reading.
pairings.quote: “Salt and camphor look alike, but taste them and they differ. Among people, too, the worthy are different. Listen, Vema.” ఉప్పు కప్పురంబు ఒక్క పోలికనుండు, చూడ చూడ రుచుల జాడ వేరు, పురుషులందు పుణ్యపురుషులు వేరయా, విశ్వదాభిరామ వినుర వేమ uppu kappurambu okka pōlikanuṇḍu, chūḍa chūḍa ruchula jāḍa vēru, puruṣulandu puṇyapuruṣulu vērayā, viśvadābhirāma vinura vēma. Vēmana, padyam (Telugu)

chapters.title: Training and Development
chapters.scope: Building skills for today's job and growing people for tomorrow's: the methods, the process and the difference between the two.

blocks.title: Training and its methods
blocks.html:
Training is a systematic process of enhancing employees' skills, knowledge and competencies to improve performance in their current job. It focuses on practical application, specific abilities and work efficiency, and it raises productivity and quality while lowering operational costs.

On-the-job methodKey focus
CoachingOne-to-one instruction in job skills
Job rotationExperience across departments or tasks
MentoringLong-term guidance by a senior
InternshipsPractical work experience
ApprenticeshipsLong-term, skill-based training

Off-the-job training takes place outside the normal work environment, through theory or simulation: classroom training, seminars and workshops, e-learning, simulation exercises and case studies.

blocks.title: The training process
blocks.html:
StepWhat happens
1 Identify training needsFind performance gaps and skill shortages
2 Determine participantsSelect the employees who need training
3 Prepare learnersBuild readiness and interest
4 Present the operationDemonstrate the task clearly
5 Performance try-outTrainees perform under supervision
6 Follow-upEvaluate, correct errors and make sure it is applied

Needs, participants, preparation, presentation, try-out, follow-up.

blocks.title: Development, and how it differs from training
blocks.html:
Development enhances employees' knowledge, skills and abilities for future responsibilities and long-term growth. It focuses on future roles, career growth, leadership potential and the talent pipeline. Its methods include training programmes, job rotation, job enrichment, mentoring and coaching, skill workshops, e-learning, cross-training, simulations and role-play, certifications, and feedback and appraisal.

TrainingDevelopment
FocusSpecific job-related skillsBroader career and personal growth
Time horizonShort-termLong-term
ScopeJob-specific and narrowCareer-oriented and wide
PurposeImprove current performancePrepare for future roles
MethodsOn-the-job training, workshops, seminarsMentoring, coaching, job rotation

Training is for current performance; development is for future growth.

text: The Kuṟaḷ says: learn thoroughly what is worth learning, and then stand by it. The training process ends the same way, with a follow-up that checks whether what was learnt is being applied.
pairings.quote: “Learn thoroughly what should be learnt, and having learnt it, live by it.” கற்க கசடறக் கற்பவை கற்றபின் நிற்க அதற்குத் தக. Tirukkuṟaḷ 391

text: The deeper a well is dug in sand, the more water flows into it; the more a person learns, the more their knowledge grows. Development, unlike training, is open-ended growth of exactly this kind.
pairings.quote: “As water springs in a sand well the deeper it is dug, so knowledge springs the more one learns.” தொட்டனைத் தூறும் மணற்கேணி மாந்தர்க்குக் கற்றனைத் தூறும் அறிவு. Tirukkuṟaḷ 396

chapters.title: Job Analysis, Evaluation and Design
chapters.scope: Studying jobs, writing them down, judging their worth and shaping them: analyse, document, evaluate, design.

blocks.title: Job analysis and its methods
blocks.html:
Job analysis is a systematic study of a job's tasks, methods, equipment, skills and attitudes needed for successful performance. It yields four kinds of information: the job's purpose and nature, its organisational fit (department, reporting line, hierarchy), the human profile it needs (skills, attributes, behaviour), and its relationships and context (interactions, dependencies, tools, demands).

Its strategic uses are work simplification (breaking complex jobs into manageable tasks), setting measurable performance standards, and supporting recruitment, selection, training and appraisal.

MethodKey focus
Direct observationWatching employees at work; best for routine or physical jobs
Work method analysisTime and motion study to find the most efficient sequence
Critical incident techniqueAnalysing exceptionally effective or ineffective incidents
Interview methodEmployees and supervisors describe the job in detail

A limit of observation: people may behave differently when watched (the Hawthorne effect).

blocks.title: Job description and job specification
blocks.html:
Job description: defines the jobJob specification: defines the person
Job purpose and summaryRequired qualifications
Tasks and dutiesExperience
Reporting line and locationMental and physical attributes
Working conditionsEmotional traits
Tools and responsibilitiesTechnical and interpersonal skills

The job description says what the job involves; the job specification says who can do it.

blocks.title: Job evaluation and its methods
blocks.html:
Job evaluation is a systematic, comparative process of determining the relative worth of jobs within an organisation. Its objectives are internal equity (jobs of similar worth get fair pay), a standard pay structure, fairness (less favouritism and wage inequality) and benchmarking against industry pay.

Job analysis → job documentation → job rating → job hierarchy
MethodKindCore idea
RankingNon-quantitativeCompare and rank jobs by overall worth
Grading or classificationNon-quantitativePlace jobs into predefined grades
Points systemQuantitativeWeight compensable factors and assign points
Factor comparisonQuantitativeCompare jobs with benchmark jobs, factor by factor

Non-quantitative methods compare whole jobs; quantitative ones score factors.

blocks.title: Job design
blocks.html:
Job design is structuring jobs to achieve organisational efficiency while meeting employees' motivational needs.

MethodWhat it does
Job simplificationFewer, repetitive tasks: more efficiency, but possible monotony
Job rotationMoves people across roles: less boredom, more versatility
Job enlargementHorizontal expansion: more tasks at the same level
Job enrichmentVertical expansion: more responsibility, autonomy and decision-making
